mainEntity.name: Why are my gums suddenly bleeding when I brush my teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bleeding when brushing is most commonly a sign of gingivitis — early-stage gum disease caused by plaque build-up along the gumline. The gum tissue becomes inflamed and more fragile, making it prone to bleeding with minimal contact. Improving brushing technique and adding daily interdental cleaning often helps reduce this over one to two weeks. If bleeding continues or worsens despite improved hygiene, it is worth discussing this with a dental professional who can assess the gum tissue and recommend appropriate care.

mainEntity.name: Can gum pain go away on its own without treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild gum discomfort caused by minor irritation — such as a food fragment caught under the gum or minor trauma — may settle without treatment once the irritant is removed. However, pain caused by gum disease, infection, or an abscess is unlikely to resolve without professional care. Leaving dental infections untreated can allow them to progress. If gum pain persists for more than a couple of days, or is severe from the outset, seeking a dental assessment is advisable.

mainEntity.name: Is gum bleeding ever a sign of something other than gum disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: Whilst gum disease is the most common reason for gum bleeding, other factors can contribute. These include certain medications (such as blood thinners), vitamin deficiencies (particularly Vitamin C or Vitamin K), hormonal changes (for example, during pregnancy), blood disorders, or vigorous brushing technique. A dental professional can examine your gums and, where appropriate, liaise with your GP if a systemic cause is suspected. Gum bleeding should always be assessed rather than assumed to be harmless.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a gum abscess and a tooth abscess?

acceptedAnswer.text: A gum abscess (periodontal abscess) forms within the gum tissue, often related to a deep periodontal pocket where bacteria have become trapped. A tooth abscess (periapical abscess) originates at the root tip of a tooth, usually as a result of untreated tooth decay or a cracked tooth allowing bacteria to reach the dental pulp. Both can cause significant pain, swelling, and localised bleeding. Both also require professional assessment; abscesses do not resolve reliably without clinical management.

mainEntity.name: Should I be worried if my gums are swollen as well as painful?

acceptedAnswer.text: Swollen, painful gums can indicate infection or significant inflammation and are worth having assessed by a dental professional, particularly if the swelling is increasing, spreading to the cheek or jaw, or accompanied by a fever, difficulty swallowing, or general unwellness. Swelling that involves areas beyond the immediate gum tissue may require more prompt evaluation. A dentist can assess the extent of swelling, identify its cause, and advise on appropriate next steps.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can gum disease become serious?

acceptedAnswer.text: The rate at which gum disease progresses varies between individuals and depends on factors including oral hygiene, smoking status, diabetes, genetics, and immune health. Gingivitis can develop within days of inadequate plaque removal, and with consistent improvement in oral hygiene, it is often reversible. Periodontitis develops more gradually over months or years, though acute episodes — such as an abscess or ANUG — can cause rapid deterioration. Regular dental check-ups are one of the most effective ways to monitor and manage gum health before problems escalate.
